chunks: Muhammad ibn Hammam and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Jumhoor all narrated from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn Jumhoor, who said: My father narrated to us from some of his companions, from al-Mufadhdhal ibn Umar, who said: Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said:
A tradition that you perceive (understand its reality) is better than ten that you narrate. Indeed, for every truth there is a reality, and for every rightness there is a light.

Then he said: By Allah, we do not consider a man from our Shias to be a jurisprudent until a mistake is made before him and he recognizes the mistake. Indeed, the Commander of the Faithful said from the pulpit of Kufa: 'There will be dark, blind, and dim seditions awaiting you, from which no one will be saved except the Nooma.' It was said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, what is the Nooma?' He said: 'It is the one who knows people but they do not know him.' And know that the earth does not remain without an authority (Hujjah) of Allah, but Allah will blind His creation from seeing him because of their injustice, oppression, and excessiveness against themselves. And if the earth were to remain for a single hour without an authority of Allah, it would sink with its people. But the authority knows people and they do not know him, just as Joseph knew people while they denied him.
Alas for (My) servants! There comes not to them a messenger but they mock at him.

key_terms.النُّومَةَ: The one who knows but is not known (referring to the Imam)
key_terms.خَبَرٌ تَدْرِيهِ: A tradition that you perceive/understand deeply

ai.seo_question: What is the meaning of 'Nooma' in Shia hadith and how does it relate to the Imam's knowledge?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (as) elevates epistemic depth over mere narration volume, defining a true Shia jurist by his ability to discern subtle errors ('Lahn'), a criterion rooted in Imam Ali’s description of the 'Nooma'—the Imam who knows his followers but is unrecognized by them. This concept of hidden recognition is central to Shia eschatology regarding the Occultation, where the Earth does not remain without a divine proof ('Hujjah'), even if people are blinded to him by their own transgressions. The narration concludes by linking this historical pattern of rejection to the Quranic lament in Surah Saba, emphasizing that the failure to recognize the Imam is a recurring spiritual tragedy.
